description: We are school students from Shpola Lyceum No. 5, Ukraine, taking part in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Dnipro). Our team works on "Abandoned but not Forgotten" — telling the story of NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. We are looking for teammates interested in space history, writing, design, illustration or web development. Beginners are welcome: we learn together and share tasks. If you enjoy storytelling and space exploration, join us!
summary: Cosmic Junkyard is an interactive online museum of the hardware NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. For more than 60 years, every mission that left Earth also left something behind: Apollo descent stages, three Lunar Roving Vehicles, seven silent Mars landers, and four spacecraft now leaving the Solar System. Most of this history is scattered across technical documents written for specialists, and no single place shows what is where. Our solution is a free single-page web application: a stylised map of the Moon, Mars and deep space, clickable markers, story cards with NASA photography, and a timeline from 1969 to today. A student chooses a world, clicks a marker and reads why the object was abandoned, what it does now and why it still matters. The project turns abstract space history into a journey and shows the real engineering trade-offs behind each abandoned machine. It runs on old computers and slow connections, needs no registration, and uses only open NASA data and imagery.
details:
What it does: Cosmic Junkyard lets a student explore the equipment NASA abandoned on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. The user picks a world, clicks a marker on the map, and opens a story card with a photograph, the mission name, the year, the reason the object was left there, its current status and one memorable fact. A timeline places every object by year, and filters narrow the collection by world and status.

How it works: the project is a single-page application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. All content is stored in a local dataset, so no server, database or login is required. The map is a stylised layout with positioned markers rather than a heavy mapping library, which keeps the page fast on weak hardware. Story cards are rendered from the dataset, so adding a new object means adding one record, not rewriting a page. The interface is in English, works offline after the first load and needs no account.

Benefits: the information already exists, but it is written for adults and scattered across mission pages, image archives and PDFs. Cosmic Junkyard collects it in one visual place for students aged 10-16 and their teachers, and gives schools ready-made material for lessons about space history and engineering.

What we hope to achieve: at launch the collection contains 12 artifacts; after the hackathon we plan to grow it to more than 50 objects, add audio stories, printable worksheets and QR codes for school exhibitions.

Tools used: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, Python (build scripts), the NASA Image and Video Library API, Netlify for hosting.
